newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Bolger bounces back from the ropes.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Bolger bounces back from the ropes.

text.p: New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger emerged victorious on Tuesday from tortuous coalition negotiations in which his political survival was at stake.
The stolid but tactically astute Bolger showed pragmatism and formidable negotiating skills to hammer out a coalition between his conservative National Party and nationalist New Zealand First.
But he will need to draw on all his reserves of patience and guile to last out a three-year term in partnership with New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, until now his bitterest rival.
"The coalition agreement stresses continued debt-responsible fiscal policy, the running of significant surpluses, repayment of debt and a focus on the productive sector," Bolger said.
"The impact of the increases in social spending will be offset by postponing the next round of tax cuts for one year."
Both National and NZ First had managed to "put aside past history" -- a reference to Peters' acrimonious split from National in 1993 -- and work in the best interests of the country, he said.
Bolger, a father of nine, was left fighting for his political life after New Zealanders voted in October in their first general election under proportional representation.

National, in power since 1990, surrendered much of its commanding lead in the polls as opponents savaged its record on health and education. Bolger was accused of running a negative and ineffectual campaign.
The centre-left Labour Party appeared the early favourite to team up in a coalition with New Zealand First -- an outcome that would have spelt the end of the road for Bolger.
Undaunted, he marshalled his forces for seven weeks of marathon negotiations and kept a virtual silence on their progress, allowing Peters and Labour to hog the headlines.
It was not the first time Bolger, 61, had been prematurely written off.

Few expected him to see out his second three-year term after snatching a one-seat majority from the 1993 election. But Bolger survived, leading majority, minority and coalition governments by turn as some of his MPs defected to form new parties.

From a deep recession in the late 1980s and early 1990s, economic growth rebounded to the highest levels in a generation. Unemployment fell to six percent, and a series of budget surpluses allowed tax to be cut.

At the same time, Bolger's government took the hatchet to New Zealand's cradle-to-grave welfare state, slashing benefits it said the country could not afford. Critics accused it of widening the gulf between rich and poor.

Bolger showed flexibility and pragmatism by moving National from an opponent of New Zealand's anti-nuclear legislation to its greatest defender, and from a detractor of Nelson Mandela's African National Congress to a friend of the new South Africa.

His round face and rural background saw his detractors nickname him "Spud" (potato), and his small campaign jet was dubbed "Spud One" in mockery of what some saw as pretensions by the leader of a country of 3.5 million people to world statesman status. Aides half-jokingly call him "the great helmsman".
Yet Bolger, a farmer of Irish Catholic ancestry who left school at 15, has shown he can hold his own on the world stage.

He was outspoken in his condemnation of French nuclear tests in the South Pacific in 1995, and his firm stewardship helped avert a Commonwealth crisis when Nigeria hanged nine human rights activists during a summit of the 52-nation group in
Auckland. Members voted promptly to suspend the African state.
